newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish rate cut seen dulling peseta strength.
newsitem.headline: Spanish rate cut seen dulling peseta strength.

text.p: Spain's 50 basis point cut in the key money rate is expected to lessen the pressure for the peseta to strengthen, avoiding the need for intervention by the central bank, dealers and analysts said on Friday.
"I have no doubts that the reduction in the key money market could lighten pressure on the peseta," said Cesar Cantalapiedra, analyst at Analistas Financieros Internacionales.
He added that the current strength of the Spanish currency was due not only to better economic fundamentals but also to the large spread between Spanish and German short-term interest rates.
Spain's key money rate is now 6.25 percent while its German counterpart has been at 3.0 percent since August.
"The more Spain narrows its short-term spread (over Germany) the less the market will be tempted to be so active in the peseta," Cantalapiedra added.
In recent months the markets have been persuaded that the Bank of Spain was opposed to any serious appreciation in the peseta/mark parity beyond the 84 level.
Every time the market forced the rate below that level, the Spanish central bank was seeing selling pesetas and buying marks and dollars, dealers said.
The Bank of Spain's foreign currency reserves have risen 54 percent since the start of the year to above $60 billion at the end of November.
"The big jump in currency reserves is clear proof that intervention has taken place," said Antonio Villarroya, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
He said the central bank was forced to intervene to protect the ability of Spanish goods to compete abroad.

In the short run analysts expect the peseta to stay in its usual range, trading between 84.10 and 84.30 versus the mark. But in the coming months it could weaken toward 84.50 or 85.00, Cantalapiedra added.
Ramon Alfonso, analyst at Banco Sabadell, said that after today's 50 basis point cut in the official rate the market would start to expect more easing in the short term.
After the 1997 budget gets final approval and if inflation declines further as expected, the Bank of Spain could continue to lower rates, Alfonso added.
At around 1350 GMT the peseta was trading around 84.20/23 versus the mark, little changed from yesterday after moving in a range between 84.19 and 84.25.
